items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: The interviewee mentions Buddy Bowling only in the context of a jazz club investigation ('find out about Buddy Bowling') and digging up his grave for an autograph, indicating no personal interaction or direct relationship.

ctx.x: Maybe I'll get in trouble by mentioning Edgar Stein but he put money in there. But this Edgar Stein had a lot to do from keeping me from getting recognition because he was a big owner in the times, picking on a long time ago. And I found out all this stuff, not recently, but in a roundabout way, things have been rounding themselves up. this Dave Stein came here, he bought the New Orleans item in. He was the same man who created the talking mule, Francis. He helped to create the talking jackasses, the New Orleans…

Aided in a better by no other than Dr. Sushant, who puts himself as a jazz historian. Now this man here, as a jazz historian, never played jazz. He says he used to sit across the road from on Basin Street and listen to Joe Oliver playing music. And there's where he got his idea from. Well now the only thing he could have heard on Basin Street, and there's many more men as old as I am, can tell you they had no music on Basin Street outside a little violin or a piano. Or they had three Negro Rhymers at Anderson's.…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: INTERVIEWER: ...He lies as to hearing Buddy Bowling play. ... And I never heard Bowling play.

ctx.x: This is from Orchestra World. Well, November 1936, letters to the editor. For the record, gentlemen, there is a correction I would like to make in the interview with me appearing in the October issue. In the third paragraph of the article, From Honky Tonk to Swing, I stated that I heard the same tune now called Tiger Rag when I was six or eight years old. Instead of the word same, I meant to say that the tune was somewhat similar to Tiger Rag. Mr. Williams has quoted same, and has put the word same in quotes, and…

Now, I just showed you the kind of propaganda that the people put out. They all knew about Tiger Rag. Now, here's a Negro. I'm going to give you his record. And if I'm wrong, then the world is wrong. This Negro lived in Plaquemine, Louisiana, at the age of about six to eight years old, worked as a shoeshine boy for Ferdinand Herbert, who operated a barbershop in Plaquemine, Louisiana. He came to New Orleans in his late teens. He lies as to hearing Buddy Bowling play. From the dates given in the second line of…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-02
items.q: He was supposed to have heard Buddy Bowling play. Buddy Bowling, according to the statistics given out by the New Orleans Jazz Club, was incarcerated in the Crazy House.

ctx.x: Before who was this came to be?

I mean Clarence Williams. You got me right that time because I'm making a mistake. I'm just telling you, I'm reading. I'm not reading. I'm telling you from my mind. Clarence Williams came to New York around 1923. The first white man he met on Broadway was me with an introduction from A.J. Perron, which you'll find in their books too. And this Negro is supposed to have her buddy bowling play. Now let me tell you about this man, who he is, where he come from. If any of you serious scholars doubt me, I was just…
